extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemakers, administrative law practitioners, policymakers, and scholars studying notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for how agencies should treat, process, weight, and respond to mass, computer-generated, and malattributed public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking. Focuses on legal standards, policy considerations, technological tools (de-duplication/OCR), and criminality/identity concerns for malattributed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance/materiality threshold for comments (HBO standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only comments which, if true, "raise points relevant to the agency’s decision and which, if adopted, would require a change in an agency’s proposed rule" cast doubt on the reasonableness of the agency’s position; "comments which themselves are purely speculative and do not disclose the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (Home Box Office v. FCC) requires some factual or policy basis for opposition; purely speculative statements need not be answered. Courts apply this to distinguish comments that require a substantive agency response from those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold of materiality (Portland Cement formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comments must be significant enough to step over a threshold requirement of materiality before any lack of agency response or consideration becomes of concern."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly cite this idea to limit the set of comments that trigger a legal obligation to respond. Materiality is the gate that turns a comment from ignorable to legally significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond in a reasoned manner to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must "respond in a reasoned manner to the comments received, to explain how the agency resolved any significant problems raised by the comments, and to show how that resolution led the agency to the ultimate rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where comments are significant/material, the agency must explain how it considered and resolved the issues raised and link that analysis to the final rule; failure to do so can render the rule arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: No obligation to respond to every comment; "the comment process is not a vote"
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are under "no obligation to take the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters," and the public comment process "is not a vote."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical majority or sheer volume does not compel agencies to adopt the most-commented-for option. Courts recognize that quantity alone does not determine reasoned decisionmaking, though numbers can be relevant in limited contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond significant only if it shows lack of consideration of relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to respond to comments is significant only insofar as it demonstrates that the agency’s decision was not "based on a consideration of the relevant factors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignoring comments per se is not automatically unlawful; the key question is whether omission indicates the agency failed to consider important aspects of the record or relevant factors in reaching its decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and reliability of comments (self-selection bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments generally do not provide a reliable metric of the views of the broader public: commenters are an entirely self-selected group and may not be representative; the group may skew toward relatively privileged participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and courts should treat raw comment counts and sentiment cautiously as they can reflect self-selection and privilege; this affects how much weight to accord aggregate comment sentiment when finalizing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of comment sophistication and source
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of sophistication in comments and the source matter: agencies place high value on hard data and empirical support; comments from business interests are often more meticulously drafted and can have greater influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical, data-backed, and technically sophisticated comments are more likely to shape agency decisions. Agencies and researchers have found commenter influence correlates with quality and source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of opinions versus factual content (three agency approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies vary: (a) opinions in comments are irrelevant—only factual content matters; (b) opinions matter insofar as they affect political perception, Hill relations, or implementation decisions; (c) opinions matter as expressions of popular sentiment and may be considered by leadership but should not be the sole factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy captures practical variation across agencies: some ignore pure opinion, some track it for political/implementation reasons, and some treat it as a signal of public sentiment while relying primarily on substantive evidence for policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of using form comments in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general bar against agencies relying on information contained in form comments; "there is no reason the Secretary was not entitled to rely on such letters in promulgating the regulations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have upheld agency reliance on form letters (Resident Councils), but agencies should be careful: wholesale ignoring of categories of comments, even if form letters, can sometimes be found unlawful if it demonstrates failure to consider important record aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-duplication (de-duping) software as a processing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: De-duping programs scan each comment, compare it to every other comment, identify degree of overlap, and group comments that appear to derive from a common source (e.g., flagging comments that are 90%+ identical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping can massively reduce processing burden by batching identical/near-identical comments. It operates on electronic text (OCR needed for paper), typically measures word-level similarity and order, and can miss near-duplicates that use synonyms or rephrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency policies on de-duping thresholds and posting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies set overlap thresholds (e.g., 90%) at which comments are flagged as part of a mass campaign; different agencies use different thresholds and none requires 100% overlap. Some agencies post only a representative example rather than all iterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold choice affects which comments are batched or individually reviewed; practices vary across agencies (FDMS tools, contractor tools, agency-specific tools). Agencies should set and document de-duping policies, and consider consequences for public record posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing rule: review unique content in batched comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When form comments are batched, agencies generally review the unique information added (e.g., a sentence about how an issue relates to a commenter) even if identical content is treated as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duping helps eliminate duplication burden, but agencies must still inspect and treat unique or partially unique comments carefully—these are more time-consuming and may require full review if they contain substantive data or arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of de-duping (synonym/rephrasing evasion and OCR quality dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: De-duping typically focuses on exact words and order; if submitters change words to synonyms or rephrase, de-duping may not recognize duplication. For paper comments, OCR quality affects the ability to de-dupe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be aware of and mitigate technological blind spots: synonym/rewrite tactics can evade detection; OCR errors can reduce effectiveness—policy choices about thresholds and manual checks remain important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of comment numbers in limited legal contexts (e.g., NEPA controversy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have sometimes looked to the number of comments (e.g., nearly 39,000) and strong criticism to find an action "controversial" under NEPA and thus requiring a full environmental impact statement; there is disagreement on this relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While comment counts usually do not determine rule substance, in contexts like NEPA the scale of public reaction can be one factor in legal tests (controversy). Agencies should not assume numbers are always irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore comments offering significant differing views (risk of arbitrary decisionmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to ignore comments that offer a differing view than the agency adopted can demonstrate that the agency "failed to consider important aspects of the administrative record" and render action arbitrary and capricious (Morales v. Lyng example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must ensure that divergent substantive viewpoints are addressed in the record; wholesale or unexplained ignoring of meaningful contrary comments risks judicial reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and policy approach to malattributed comments (identity falsehoods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments involve a direct falsehood about the submitter's identity and may harm individuals whose names are used; whether such submissions constitute a crime is central to determining appropriate agency response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If malattribution constitutes criminal conduct, agencies should refer significant instances to DOJ, have stronger obligations to prevent/deter it, and treat the problem as more serious. Agencies and Congress have debated criminal investigations and legislative guidance; agencies should weigh identity-theft harms and legal remedies.
